--- title: "Model conditions + diagnostics" author: "Prof. Maria Tackett" date: "October 15, 2026" date-format: "MMM DD, YYYY" footer: "[🔗 sta221-fa26.github.io](https://sta221-fa26.github.io)" logo: "../images/logo.png" format: revealjs: theme: slides.scss multiplex: false transition: fade slide-number: true incremental: false chalkboard: true include-before: [ ''] html: output-file: 14-conditions-diagnostics-notes.html html-math-method: method: mathjax url: "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/mathjax@3/es5/tex-mml-chtml.js" execute: freeze: auto echo: true knitr: opts_chunk: R.options: width: 200 bibliography: references.bib --- ## Announcements - SSMU Data Challenge - October 17. See [Ed Discussion](https://edstem.org/us/courses/101204/discussion/8366022) for details - Travelers University Modeling Competition - register by October 22. See [Ed Discussion](https://edstem.org/us/courses/101204/discussion/8395549) for details ## Exam 01 - Submit regrade requests by **tomorrow, October 16 at 11:59pm** - Please review solutions before submitting a regrade request - Final exam improvement incentive (see [syllabus)](https://sta221-fa26.github.io/syllabus.html#exams)\ *For students who take all three exams, the final exam score will replace the lower of the two mid-term scores, if the final exam score is higher than the Exam 01 and/or Exam 02 score.* ## Icebreaker ::: question What is something that has brought you joy or made you laugh lately? ::: - Share in groups of 2 - 3 - We'll get some students to share with the class. ## Computing set up ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # load packages library(tidyverse) library(tidymodels) library(knitr) library(patchwork) library(viridis) # set default theme in ggplot2 ggplot2::theme_set(ggplot2::theme_bw(base_size = 16)) ``` ::: ## Topics - Model conditions - Influential points - Model diagnostics - Leverage - Standardized residuals - Cook's Distance ## Data: Duke lemurs ::: {.cell} ::: ::: midi Today’s data contains a subset of the original Duke Lemur data set available in the [TidyTuesday GitHub repo](https://github.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/blob/master/data/2021/2021-08-24/readme.md). This data includes information on 252 lemurs less than 24 months old from three taxa: - Eulemur rufus (ERUF), commonly known as Red-fronted brown lemur - Propithecus coquereli (PCOQ), commonly known as Coquerel’s sifaka - Varecia rubra (VRUB), commonly known as Red ruffed lemur. ::: **We will explore the model conditions and diagnostics for a model of weight using age and taxon.** ## Univariate EDA ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](14-conditions-diagnostics_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-3-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ## Bivariate EDA ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](14-conditions-diagnostics_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-4-1.png){fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: ## Fit model ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} |term | estimate| std.error| statistic| p.value| |:-----------|--------:|---------:|---------:|-------:| |(Intercept) | -17.270| 87.968| -0.196| 0.845| |age | 137.550| 4.824| 28.515| 0.000| |taxonPCOQ | 463.997| 94.728| 4.898| 0.000| |taxonVRUB | 999.722| 92.148| 10.849| 0.000| ::: ::: # Model conditions ## Linear regression model $$\begin{aligned} \mathbf{y} = \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta} + \boldsymbol{\epsilon}, \hspace{8mm} \boldsymbol{\epsilon} \sim N(\mathbf{0}, \sigma^2\mathbf{I}) \end{aligned} $$ such that the errors are independent and normally distributed. - **Independent**: Knowing the error term for one observation doesn't tell us about the error term for another observation - **Normally distributed**: The distribution follows a particular mathematical model that is unimodal and symmetric - $E(\boldsymbol{\epsilon}) = \mathbf{0}$ - $Var(\boldsymbol{\epsilon}) = \sigma^2\mathbf{I}$ ## Assumptions for regression $$ \mathbf{y}|\mathbf{X} \sim N(\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}, \sigma^2\mathbf{I}) $$ ![Image source: Introduction to the Practice of Statistics (5th ed)](images/08/regression.png){fig-align="center"} ## Assumptions for regression {.midi} $$ \mathbf{y}|\mathbf{X} \sim N(\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}, \sigma^2\mathbf{I}) $$ 1. **Linearity:** There is a linear relationship between the response and predictor variables. 2. **Equal variance:** The variability about the least squares line is generally constant. 3. **Normality:** The distribution of the errors (residuals) is approximately normal. 4. **Independence:** The errors (residuals) are independent from one another. . . . ::: question After fitting a model, we check a set of conditions to evaluate whether these assumptions hold for the data. ::: ## Augment data set ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} lemurs_aug <- augment(lemurs_fit) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 10 × 9 weight age taxon .fitted .resid .hat .sigma .cooksd .std.resid 1 410 2.27 ERUF 295. 115. 0.0244 534. 0.000299 0.219 2 137 0.72 ERUF 81.8 55.2 0.0263 534. 0.0000745 0.105 3 206 0.69 PCOQ 542. -336. 0.0153 533. 0.00157 -0.635 4 185 1.05 PCOQ 591. -406. 0.0149 533. 0.00223 -0.768 5 373 2.66 PCOQ 813. -440. 0.0132 533. 0.00231 -0.831 6 200 0.76 ERUF 87.3 113. 0.0262 534. 0.000310 0.214 7 1861 9.01 ERUF 1222. 639. 0.0208 532. 0.00782 1.21 8 1634 8.02 ERUF 1086. 548. 0.0209 533. 0.00577 1.04 9 636 2.76 ERUF 362. 274. 0.0239 533. 0.00165 0.520 10 373 1.74 ERUF 222. 151. 0.0250 534. 0.000528 0.287 ``` ::: ::: ## Linearity {.midi} - Examine plot of residuals versus fitted (predicted) values - Good practice to also check plots of residuals versus quantitative predictors - Linearity is satisfied if there is no discernible pattern in the plots (i.e., points randomly scattered around $\text{residuals} = 0$)
::: {.cell layout-align="center"} :::
::: question Why does seeing no discernible pattern mean linearity is satisfied? ::: ## Linearity {.midi} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](14-conditions-diagnostics_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-9-1.png){fig-align='center' width=75%} ::: ::: . . . ::: question Is linearity satisfied? ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: ## Equal variance {.midi} - Examine plot of residuals versus fitted (predicted) values - Equal variance is satisfied if the vertical spread of the points is approximately equal for all fitted values . . . ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](14-conditions-diagnostics_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-11-1.png){fig-align='center' width=50%} ::: ::: ::: question Is equal variance satisfied? ::: ## Example: Equal variance not satisfied ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Plot made from simulated data produced by ChatGPT](14-conditions-diagnostics_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-12-1.png){fig-align='center' width=75%} ::: ::: . . . - Equal variance is critical for reliable inference. Why? - Address violations by applying transformation on the response ## Example: Equal variance not satisfied ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](14-conditions-diagnostics_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-13-1.png){width=75%} ::: ::: ::: question Is linearity satisfied in this example? ::: ## Normality {.midi} - Look at the distribution of the residuals - Normality is satisfied if the distribution is approximately unimodal and symmetric. - Even if normality is not satisfied, inference is robust for $n > 30$ ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](14-conditions-diagnostics_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-14-1.png){fig-align='center' width=65%} ::: ::: . . . ::: question Is normality satisfied? ::: ## Normal Q-Q plot - An alternative way to assess normality is by examining a Normal Q-Q Plot. - The distribution of residuals is approximately normal if the points lie along the diagonal line ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true"} ggplot(lemurs_aug, aes(sample = .resid)) + stat_qq() + stat_qq_line(color = "red") + labs( title = "Normal Q-Q Plot", x = "Theoretical Quantiles", y = "Residual Quantiles" ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](14-conditions-diagnostics_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-15-1.png){fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: ## Independence - We can often check the independence condition based on the context of the data and how the observations were collected. - If the data were collected in a particular order, examine a scatterplot of the residuals versus order in which the data were collected. - If data has spatial element, plot residuals on a map to examine potential spatial correlation. - Can also check for dependence within subgroups that are not accounted for in the model ## Independence Let's check whether there is unaccounted dependence by `sex`. ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](14-conditions-diagnostics_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-16-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ::: question Is the independence condition satisfied? ::: ## Example of spatial correlation Below is a visualization of the residuals for a model of the relationship between political leanings and percentage of in-person votes cast in the 2020 election. ![](images/clipboard-4197877067.png){fig-align="center" width="75%"} ::: question What would the map look like if independence was satisfied? Is the condition satisfied? ::: ## Example of correlation over time ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Simulation produced by ChatGPT GPT-6 Astra](14-conditions-diagnostics_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-17-1.png){fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: ## Your turn ::: question Which condition(s) must be satisfied for a linear regression model to produce reliable predictions? Select all that apply. ::: ![](images/october-15-qrcode.png){fig-align="center" width="30%"} ::: center ::: # Model diagnostics ## Model diagnostics in R {.midi} We get observation-level model diagnostics from `augment()` in R. We will use the following columns: - `.hat`: leverage - `.cooksd`: Cook's distance - `.std.resid`: standardized residuals ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 5 × 10 weight age taxon .fitted .resid .hat .sigma .cooksd .std.resid sex 1 410 2.27 ERUF 295. 115. 0.0244 534. 0.000299 0.219 F 2 137 0.72 ERUF 81.8 55.2 0.0263 534. 0.0000745 0.105 F 3 206 0.69 PCOQ 542. -336. 0.0153 533. 0.00157 -0.635 F 4 185 1.05 PCOQ 591. -406. 0.0149 533. 0.00223 -0.768 M 5 373 2.66 PCOQ 813. -440. 0.0132 533. 0.00231 -0.831 F ``` ::: ::: ## Influential point An observation is **influential** if removing has a noticeable impact on the regression coefficients ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](14-conditions-diagnostics_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-19-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ## Influential points ::: incremental - Influential points have a noticeable impact on the coefficients and their standard errors - These points can sometimes be identified in a scatterplot if there is only one predictor variable - This is often not the case when there are multiple predictors - We will use measures to quantify an individual observation's influence on the regression model - **leverage**, **standardized residuals**, and **Cook's Distance** ::: # Cook's Distance ## Motivating Cook's Distance - An observation's influence on the regression line depends on - How close it lies to the general trend of the data - Its leverage - **Cook's Distance** is a statistic that includes both of these components to measure an observation's overall impact on the model ## Cook's Distance Cook's distance for the $i^{th}$ observation is $$ D_i = \frac{r^2_i}{p + 1}\Big(\frac{h_{ii}}{1 - h_{ii}}\Big) $$ where $r_i$ is the standardized residual and $h_{ii}$ is the leverage for the $i^{th}$ observation . . . This measure is a combination of - How well the model fits the $i^{th}$ observation (magnitude of residuals) - How far the $i^{th}$ observation is from the rest of the data ## Using Cook's Distance - An observation with large value of $D_i$ is said to have a strong influence on the predicted values - General thresholds .An observation with - $D_i > 0.5$ is **moderately influential** - $D_i > 1$ is **very influential** ## Cook's Distance Cook's Distance is in the column `.cooksd` in the output from `augment()` ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](14-conditions-diagnostics_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-20-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ## Comparing models {.midi} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} |Term | All obs| -Max(Cook's D)| |:-----------|-------:|--------------:| |(Intercept) | -17.270| 19.583| |age | 137.550| 133.392| |taxonPCOQ | 463.997| 423.287| |taxonVRUB | 999.722| 1003.960| ::: :::
Model coefficients do not change much because there are no influential points in the data. # Leverage ## Leverage {.midi} ::: incremental - Recall the **hat matrix** $\mathbf{H} = \mathbf{X}(\mathbf{X}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^\mathsf{T}$ - We focus on the diagonal elements $$ h_{ii} = \mathbf{x}_i^\mathsf{T}(\mathbf{X}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{x}_i $$such that $\mathbf{x}^\mathsf{T}_i$ is the $i^{th}$ row of $\mathbf{X}$ - $h_{ii}$ is the **leverage**: measures how far an observation’s predictor values are from the mean predictor values - It measures how much $\hat{y}_i$ changes when $y_i$ changes, holding the values of the predictor constant ::: ## High leverage ::: incremental - The sum of the leverages for all points is $p + 1$, where $p$ is the number of predictors in the model . More specifically $$ \sum_{i=1}^n h_{ii} = \text{rank}(\mathbf{H}) = \text{rank}(\mathbf{X}) = p+1 $$ - The average value of leverage, $h_{ii}$, is $\bar{h} = \frac{(p+1)}{n}$ - An observation has **high leverage** if $$h_{ii} > \frac{2(p+1)}{n}$$ ::: ## Lemurs: Leverage ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} h_threshold <- 2 * (3 + 1) / nrow(lemurs) h_threshold ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.03174603 ``` ::: ::: . . . ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} lemurs_aug |> filter(.hat > h_threshold) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 5 × 10 weight age taxon .fitted .resid .hat .sigma .cooksd .std.resid sex 1 2515 20.6 ERUF 2823. -308. 0.0322 533. 0.00288 -0.588 F 2 2230 22.2 ERUF 3031. -801. 0.0353 531. 0.0215 -1.53 F 3 1776. 20.6 ERUF 2818. -1042. 0.0322 529. 0.0328 -1.99 F 4 1761 23.0 ERUF 3144. -1383. 0.0372 526. 0.0676 -2.65 F 5 2040 22.2 ERUF 3031. -991. 0.0353 530. 0.0328 -1.89 F ``` ::: :::
. . . ::: question Why do you think these points have high leverage? ::: ## Let's look at the data ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](14-conditions-diagnostics_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-24-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ## High leverage If there is point with high leverage, ask - ❓ Is there a data entry error? - ❓ Is this observation within the scope of individuals for which you want to make predictions and draw conclusions? - ❓ Is this observation impacting the estimates of the model coefficients? (Need more information!) . . . Just because a point has high leverage does not necessarily mean it will have a substantial impact on the regression. Therefore we need to check other measures. # Standardized residuals ## Standardized residuals ::: incremental - What is the best way to identify outlier points that don't fit the pattern from the regression line? - Look for points that have large residuals - We can rescale residuals and put them on a common scale to more easily identify "large" residuals ::: ## Standardized residuals {.midi} ::: incremental - The variance of the residuals is $Var(\mathbf{e}) = \sigma^2(\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{H})$ - The variance of the $i^{th}$ residual is $Var(e_i) = \sigma^2(1 - h_{ii})$ - The **standardized residual** (also called internally studentized residual)is the residual rescaled by its variance ::: $$ r_i = \frac{e_{i}}{\sqrt{\hat{\sigma}^2(1 - h_{ii})}} $$ ## Using standardized residuals - We can use the standardized residuals in the plot of residuals versus predicted - Use it to evaluate linearity, equal variance, and outliers - An observation is a *potential outlier* if its standardized residual has magnitude greater than 3 ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](14-conditions-diagnostics_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-25-1.png){fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: ## Using these measures - Standardized residuals, leverage, and Cook's Distance should all be examined together - Examine plots of the measures to identify observations that are outliers, high leverage, and may potentially impact the model. ## Diagnostic plots using gglm Can make main diagnostic plots using `gglm()` in the **gglm** R package ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(gglm) gglm(lemurs_fit) ``` :::
**gglm** documentation:
::: callout-tip You will need to install this package in RStudio in the Docker containers. ::: ## Diagnostic plots using gglm ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](14-conditions-diagnostics_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-27-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ## What to do with outliers/influential points? ::: incremental - First consider if the outlier is a result of a data entry error. - If not, you may consider dropping an observation if it's an outlier in the predictor variables if... - It is meaningful to drop the observation given the context of the problem - You intended to build a model on a smaller range of the predictor variables. Mention this in the write up of the results and be careful to avoid extrapolation when making predictions ::: ## What to do with outliers/influential points? ::: incremental - It is generally **not** good practice to drop observations that ar outliers in the value of the response variable - These are legitimate observations and should be in the model - You can try transformations or increasing the sample size by collecting more data - A general strategy when there are influential points is to fit the model with and without the influential points and compare the outcomes ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Recap - Model conditions - Influential points - Model diagnostics - Leverage - Standardized residuals Cook's Distance ## Before next class - Multicollinearity - Complete [Lecture 15 prepare](../prepare/prepare-lec15.html)

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
